description.value: The study examined how reward-context information is learned and integrated with sensory evidence during perceptual motion decisions using reinforcement-learning models and fMRI, including mass-univariate GLM and PPI analyses.

spans.text: We addressed these questions using model-based neuroimaging in a motion discrimination paradigm where contextual cues suggested which one of two options would receive higher rewards on each trial.

design.value: During fMRI acquisition, participants performed a motion discrimination task with pre-trial cues signaling one of two different reward contexts and trial-wise reward feedback, analyzed with reinforcement-learning model-based fMRI and psychophysiological interaction analyses.

task_description.value: Participants decided whether the global motion direction of moving dots was upward or downward in two independent reward contexts, with reward feedback after each trial.

spans.text: In the scanner, participants were asked to decide the motion direction of moving-dots presented in two independent reward contexts with a goal to get as many reward points as possible over the experiment.

description.value: FMRI data preprocessing included motion correction, bad-time-point identification, skull stripping, spatial smoothing, grand-mean intensity normalization, high-pass filtering, and registration to MNI-152 space.

spans.text: FMRI data preprocessing was carried out using FSL Version 5.0.1 (FMRIB's Software Library: www.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/ ).

software.value: FSL Version 5.0.1; FreeSurfer; SPM deconvolution algorithm

spans.text: FMRI data preprocessing was carried out using FSL Version 5.0.1 (FMRIB's Software Library: www.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/ ).

steps.value: MCFLIRT alignment; FD and DVARS calculation; BET skull stripping; FreeSurfer structural skull stripping; 5 mm FWHM Gaussian smoothing; grand-mean intensity normalization; high-pass temporal filtering with sigma = 50.0 s; functional-to-structural BBR registration; structural-to-MNI-152 2 mm FLIRT registration.

spans.text: All image time series were aligned with the MCFLIRT tool, and the resulting motion parameters were used to compute frame-wise displacement (FD) and temporal derivative of the root mean square variance over voxels (DVARS) to identify bad time points ( FD > 0.5; DVARS > 0.5) (Power et al., ). The skull was removed from the functional images with the brain extraction tool (BET) and from the structural images using FreeSurfer ( https://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/ ). Spatial smoothing was applied using a Gaussian kernel of FWHM 5 mm. The grand-mean intensity was normalized over the entire 4D dataset by a single multiplicative factor, and a high-pass temporal filtering (Gaussian-weighted least-squares straight line fitting, with sigma = 50.0 s).
We used multi-stage general linear model (GLM) approach to analyze the brain imaging data, using FSL FEAT (FMRI Expert Analysis Tool) Version 6.00.
All the regressors except the motion-correction regressors in the first-level model were convolved with a double-gamma hemodynamic response function.

model_settings.value: First-level models were estimated separately for each run and participant; runs were combined within participant using fixed effects; group-level analysis used FLAME 1 mixed effects. Parametric regressors included absolute coherence, trial-wise bias, and reward prediction error; nuisance regressors included trial-evoked activity, reaction time, motion parameters, FD, DVARS, and scrubbed time points.

model_settings.value: Three independent PPI analyses used seed regions in frontal cortex, parietal cortex, and vmPFC; each model included the GLM design matrix plus the raw seed time course and a PPI regressor.

spans.text: The above-mentioned brain areas (i.e., frontal, parietal, and value systems) are selected according to the previous literature and used as the seed regions in three independent PPI analyses.
For each individual and each run, the neural signal of the seed region was estimated by deconvolving the BOLD signals using the deconvolution algorithm of SPM (Gitelman et al., ).
